newsitem.title: USA: Compromise on N.J. pension deal seen taking shape.
newsitem.headline: Compromise on N.J. pension deal seen taking shape.

text.p: A compromise may be taking shape on the Whitman Administration's plan to borrow $2.75 billion to bolster New Jersey's public employee pension funds, legislative sources said Tuesday.
Whitman wants to use the bonds to fully fund the state's pension system, saving almost $600 million in a related maneuver to balance next year's budget.

The idea has so far stalled in the state Senate, where legislators, many of whom face an election battle in November, fear the public will not understand the complex deal and see it simply as a budget gimmick.

But with revenues coming in far above forecast, lawmakers said Tuesday they may be able to agree to a bond deal that features a budgetary component smaller than the $600 million now under consideration.
Sen. John Matheussen, for example, said that only a bond issue with less benefit for the budget could pass the Senate.
State Treasurer Brian Clymer, who is planning to testify Wednesday on updated revenue figures, may have enough good news to allow that to happen.

Through April, New Jersey's tax revenues are about $167 million over projections, and are on track to end the fiscal year on June 30 about $250 million over forecast. Whitman has hinted the figure might be high enough to allow her to lower the budget impact of her bond proposal, even as the state maintains its expected $550 million budget surplus.
She said that would enable legislators to vote on the merits of the bond issue. How much the budget impact would shrink depends on how good the treasurer's news is on Wednesday.
New Jersey earlier this year selected Merrill Lynch & Co to underwrite the bonds if the deal wins legislative approval.
